title: Errors in an analytics tool
excerpt: When a chart fails, say whether the last number is still safe to cite, how old it is, and the one recovery. Leave a stale figure unlabeled and people will repeat it.
alt: A close view of a fountain pen writing on lined paper, the sentence that should sit beside a number that failed to refresh.
caption: Write the failure in words a meeting can repeat. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an analytics error tell the operator?
faqs.answer: Whether the number is current, whether it is the last good refresh and how old that is, or whether it is not safe to cite. Put that sentence on the number. A timeout in a corner toast will be cropped out of the screenshot they paste into a deck.

faqs.question: Should the whole page fail if one chart fails?
faqs.answer: No. Mark the chart that failed and leave a good headline standing. If the headline itself failed, do not replace it with a zero. Offer a narrower question when the query was too wide, and name the role limit when the viewer may see a total but not the rows.

faqs.question: How should a late refresh be described?
faqs.answer: Say the number is incomplete or late, and name the last complete window, with one tap to view it. That is different from a disconnected source, which needs a reconnect by someone who is allowed to do it. Do not use one sentence for both.

markdown:
Honest analytics tool error states tell the operator what broke, whether the last good number is still safe to use, and what to do next. A code and a sad chart waste the moment they opened the tool to make a decision.

The W3C's WCAG overview groups the guidelines under perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. An error has to be readable as text, and understandable as a next step. A red widget with no sentence fails both.

## Say whether the number can be trusted

This is the line most analytics screens skip. The operator does not need your stack trace. They need to know if they may repeat the figure in the room they are about to enter.

Use one of three statuses, in words:

- The number is current.
- The number is the last good refresh, and you are saying how old it is.
- The number is not safe to cite, and you are saying why.

"Couldn't load" with a blank where the figure was is the third status, but only if you also remove the stale figure or mark it. Leaving yesterday's revenue on screen, unlabelled, while a toast says the query failed, is how a wrong number escapes into a forecast.

Put the sentence on the number, not in a corner. If one tile failed and three succeeded, mark the one. Do not fail the whole page because a secondary chart timed out. The headline they came for should survive a broken decoration. If the headline itself failed, say so, and do not fill the space with a zero.

Include the window and the source in the failure, the same way you include them in the success. "Paid invoices for the last 7 days did not refresh. The figure below is from 6:40 am." That sentence can be read aloud. "GraphQL error: timeout" cannot.

## Name the kind of break

Operators can act on a short list of causes. Write those, and map the ugly causes onto them.

A disconnected source. The warehouse, the billing tool, or the product database stopped authorizing you. The fix is to reconnect, and the person who can do that may not be the person looking at the screen. Say both. "The billing connection expired. A workspace owner can reconnect it." If this viewer cannot, do not show a button that fails.

A late or partial refresh. The number exists and is incomplete. "US settlements usually arrive by 8:00. Today's are not in yet. Yesterday's total is complete." Partial is a different recovery from failed. Offer to view the last complete day in one tap.

A query that is too heavy. The window or the breakdown they asked for did not return in time. Say that the question was too wide, and offer a narrower one that you know works. "Try 7 days instead of 12 months," or "Drop the city breakdown." A retry button that repeats the impossible query is not a recovery.

A permission gap. They can see the dashboard and not the rows. That should read as a limit, not as a broken chart. "You can see the total. Customer-level rows are limited to your region." Send them toward the explanation of roles, not toward a generic failure.

A bug. You do not know. Say that you do not know, keep the last good number labeled, and give them a way to tell a human. A reference they can quote is useful. A reference as the only text is not.

## Do not punish the refresh

A manual refresh should be safe and honest. If they tap it, show that you are working, and do not fire five more queries because the button stayed live. When the new number arrives, say that it arrived. When it does not, keep the previous labeled figure and add the failure. Never clear a trusted number to show a spinner and then fail back to empty.

Scheduled refreshes fail overnight. The morning screen should lead with that, if it happened, before the operator copies the figure into a note. Email and chat alerts can repeat the sentence. They should not be the only place the sentence exists. The person who opens the tool at 9:00 should see it without hunting a notification they dismissed.

Backfills and restatements are not quite errors, but they break trust the same way if you hide them. When late data changes a day you already showed, mark the day. "6 April was updated after a backfill." An operator who screenshotted the old number needs to see that the change was real and intentional. Otherwise they will treat every future change as a defect.

## The drill-down can fail alone

Often the headline is fine and the rows underneath are not. Let the headline stand. On the table, say which part failed. "The plan breakdown did not load. The total above is still the last good refresh." Offer to retry the breakdown without reloading the whole page and losing their scroll, their filter, and their nerve.

Exports fail too. If a CSV did not build, the on-screen number is still what it was. Say that. "The file did not generate. The figure on this page is unchanged." Then offer a smaller export if the full one is the thing that times out. A failed download that makes people doubt the page is an error of copy, not only of infrastructure.

Filters can be the failure. A combination that matches nothing is an empty state, not a server error, and it should say the filters are the reason. A combination you cannot compute is an error, and it should say which filter to relax. Mixing those two messages trains people to ignore both.

## Write the sentences before the illustrations

Make a list of the failures your pipeline can actually produce, and write the operator-facing sentence for each one before anyone draws an empty chart. A practical set:

- The source needs to be reconnected, and this role can or cannot do it.
- The refresh is late, and the last complete window is named.
- This chart timed out, and a narrower question is offered.
- This viewer may see the total and not the rows.
- You are not sure, the last good number is labeled, and a person can be told.

Read them out loud next to the figure. If you cannot say whether the number is citable, the sentence is unfinished. If two causes share one sentence, split them. The recovery is different, so the words are different.

Check the visual order. The sentence comes first. Color can reinforce it. An illustration can exist if it does not push the sentence below the fold on a laptop. A mascot with a wrench, and the real words in small type underneath, repeats the mistake this screen exists to avoid.

## The meeting that is about to quote it

Assume the broken number will be screenshotted. Design the failure so the screenshot still contains the caveat. If the warning is a toast, it will be gone. If it is a banner above a different chart, the crop will miss it. The sentence has to sit in the same frame as the digits. "Last good refresh, 6:40 am, billing connection expired" should be readable in the image they paste into the deck.

Give the operator a copy action that includes the caveat, the way a healthy screen's copy includes the window. Copying only the digits from a warned chart is how the warning dies at the boundary of the tool. If they copy, copy the truth. If the number is not safe to cite at all, the copy action can refuse and say why, in the same sentence already on the screen.

After the meeting, the same sentence should still be there. Do not clear warnings on a timer. Clear a warning when the refresh succeeds, and say that it succeeded. "Updated 9:12 am. This figure is current." An operator who returns after lunch should not have to remember whether the morning's number was the bad one. The screen remembers.

## Where it goes next

Some of these "errors" are permissions wearing a failure costume. The operator can open the report and cannot see the customers inside it. Treating that as a timeout will make them retry all morning. [Permissions in an analytics tool](/blog/permissions-in-an-analytics-tool) is the next piece, because the screen should say what this role is allowed to see, and why the rest is absent.

Hanabi writes these states with the first screen, in Figma, using figures that look like money and counts rather than gray boxes. The build is Next.js, React, and TypeScript. The last good number, the freshness, and the reason string should be real fields, not a banner someone pasted on after the incident. PostgreSQL and Prisma are a reasonable home for that record so the page can tell the truth after a bad refresh.

If your charts fail into codes, or into a blank where a citable number used to be, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the last error your team actually hit and the decision that was waiting on it. The call should produce the sentence the screen ought to have shown.
